# Smooth fiber boundary pairing without an isolated-crossing assumption

This note strengthens the scoped crossing theorem in
`candidate 1082ab3797f11f8f` when
the continuous dimension is at least three. It does not show that an
arbitrary attained minimizer has strict compatibility or smooth fibers.
It also does not identify fiberwise paired planes with ambient paired
planes.

## 1. Strict compatibility exposes every strictly exposed own point

Use the finite positive actual family and strict compatibility hypothesis
of `candidate 97eab0f821e54041`.
Fix a base q and a unit continuous normal u. Suppose its support face in
K_q is the singleton {v}. Then (q,v) is globally exposed in the ambient
hull C.

Here is a finite-dimensional proof, including nonextreme integer bases.
Put s_p=h_(K_p)(u). We seek an integer-coordinate coefficient a with

    a.(p-q)+s_p-s_q<0 for all p!=q.                       (1)

Consider the compact convex hull X of the finitely many vectors
(p-q,s_p-s_q) in R^(n+1). It is disjoint from the ray
R={0} x [0,infinity): a point of X with first coordinate zero is an
anchored convex combination of other bases, and strict compatibility
puts its last coordinate strictly below zero. If there are no other bases,
the conclusion is immediate.

The compact set X and closed ray R have positive distance and admit a
strict separating functional (a,c) with sup_X(a,c).x<inf_R(a,c).r.
The latter infimum is finite only if c>=0, and is then zero. If c=0,
replace c by a sufficiently small positive number: finiteness of the
original vertex list preserves all the strict inequalities. Divide by c
to obtain (1). The functional (p,x)->a.p+u.x is then uniquely maximized
at (q,v). This proves the claim using the original coordinates.

Consequently, if K_q is C1 and strictly convex, every point of its boundary
satisfies the exposure and singleton-normal requirements of the signed
local-mass theorem. No separate assumption that q is an exposed lattice
base is needed.

## 2. A geometric pairing lemma on a strictly convex boundary

Let K be a C1 strictly convex body in R^d with d>=3, and let U be a
nonempty relatively open subset of boundary K. Consider finitely many
oriented continuous halfspaces H_j with nonzero normals and weights
omega_j>=0. Suppose

    sum_j omega_j 1_H_j(x)=b

for every x in U off their boundary hyperplanes. Then for every unoriented
hyperplane L which meets U and properly cuts K, the total weight of the
halfspaces with boundary L in either orientation is the same:

    sum_(boundary H_j=L, positive orientation) omega_j
       =sum_(boundary H_j=L, negative orientation) omega_j.       (2)

Only planes actually present in the finite list matter. A plane which
does not meet U imposes no such constraint from this patch.

### Proof that an unshared crossing point exists

The section D=K intersect L is a (d-1)-dimensional strictly convex body in
L. Its boundary in L is T=boundary K intersect L. Every intersection is
transverse: otherwise the continuous normal of L would be parallel to
the unique supporting normal of K at that point, making L a supporting
plane, contrary to its properly cutting K. Thus T is a C1 hypersurface
in L of dimension d-2>=1.

For any different hyperplane L', the closed set T intersect L' has empty
relative interior in T. Otherwise an open C1 patch of T would lie in
the proper affine hyperplane L intersect L' of L. Its dimension is at
most d-2. At any point of that patch its tangent space has dimension
d-2 and is contained in this affine hyperplane's direction space, so
the dimensions are equal. The inverse function theorem applied to its
projection onto that affine hyperplane then makes the patch contain a
relatively open subset of the hyperplane. Such a subset contains a line
segment. This contradicts strict convexity of D, since that segment would
lie in its boundary. Parallel disjoint L' have empty intersection from
the outset.

Each of the finitely many other planes therefore removes a closed set
with empty interior from T. Their complements are open dense sets; a
finite intersection of these is dense. Hence the nonempty relatively open
set T intersect U contains a point v on none of the other planes. This
step uses finiteness, not an unstated genericity assumption.

At v the plane L crosses U transversely, and all other cap planes have a
fixed strict margin. Take nearby points x^+ and x^- in U on opposite
sides. Only halfspaces with boundary L change incidence, with signs
according to their orientations. Subtracting the two constant-score
equations gives exactly (2). This proves the geometric lemma.

## 3. Consequence for the selected critical circuit stress

Retain the finite critical circuits, equal positive threshold slopes, and
weights kappa_pj of the two preceding notes. Assume an unrestricted local
minimum in the strictly compatible phase. Let U_q be any finite collection
of C1 strictly convex feasible boundary patches, each in its indicated
fiber. In particular entire C1 strictly convex fiber boundaries are allowed.

There is ONE probability vector pi on the selected deepest bases such
that, for every selected fiber q and every proper restricted cap plane L
meeting U_q,

    sum_p pi_p sum_(j: H_pj|q has plane L, +) kappa_pj
       =sum_p pi_p sum_(j: H_pj|q has plane L, -) kappa_pj.       (3)

There is no additional isolated-crossing hypothesis in this assertion.
One way to prove it is to use Section 2 to select a crossing pair for
each of the finitely many relevant restricted planes in each chosen fiber,
then apply the signed theorem to their union. The single resulting pi
satisfies all jump equations (3).

Equivalently, the constant-score hypothesis of Section 2 can be obtained
without an infinite compactness argument. Across all these patches there
are only finitely many incidence patterns for the finite selected cap
list, at most 2^N if the list has N caps. Choose one feasible point for
every realized pattern off the planes and apply the signed theorem once.
The resulting pi gives score beta at every point off the planes with a
realized pattern. Applying Section 2 with omega_pj=pi_p kappa_pj gives (3).

If every fiber is strictly convex and d>=2, the equality of the threshold
traces required here is automatic: a supporting section is at most a
singleton and has zero (d-1)-dimensional measure; proper sections have
continuous area. Each critical cap's own proper anchor section supplies
a strictly positive common slope. C1 smoothness is used above for the
exposure and transversality arguments, not to discard coincident facet
mass in fibers which might have facets.

### Full-boundary counting consequence

If an entire fiber K_q has the required smooth strict convexity, every
proper restricted cap plane is covered. Let F_q be the total stress weight
pi_p kappa_pj of caps containing its entire boundary off their planes,
and let P_q be the total such weight of properly cutting caps. Tangent
caps contribute a constant zero or one off their contact point and are
included in the appropriate constant class. Equation (3) makes every
proper opposite pair contribute half its total weight. Thus

    beta=F_q+P_q/2.                                      (4)

In particular, for q a deepest base, every cap of q's own selected
circuit properly cuts its fiber through its interior center. Its total
stress weight is pi_q, so P_q>=pi_q. Therefore

    pi_q<=2 beta.

If all deepest fibers satisfy the full-boundary hypotheses, summing over
their finite set I gives beta>=1/(2|I|).

This numerical consequence already appears in a different smooth-variation
form in `candidate 23c5cf376b5f9d55`. The present proof
does not require a unique sharp center or differentiating an infinite
active family. It follows from exact finite circuit covers and realized
local mass changes. There is still no proved bound on |I| that would
convert it into (OC), and no claim that this open compatibility phase
contains an attained global minimizer.

## 4. Why d=2 is different

On the unit circle in R^2 take

    u_1=(1,0),
    u_2=(-1/2,sqrt(3)/2),
    u_3=(-1/2,-sqrt(3)/2),
    H_i={x:u_i.x>=1/2}.

Each cap traces a closed arc of angular length 2pi/3. Their interiors
partition the circle; the only overlaps are the three shared endpoints.
Thus with omega_i=1/3 the score is exactly 1/3 at every circle point off
the three boundary lines. No two lines coincide and none is an opposite
orientation of another. At a crossing endpoint another distinct line
necessarily crosses too. The section trace now has dimension zero, so
the empty-interior argument from Section 2 is unavailable.

This is an exact obstruction to inferring opposite-plane pairing from
constant boundary score alone in d=2. It is not asserted to be a critical
circuit configuration of a mixed-integer local minimizer.

## 5. Fiberwise pairing does not mean ambient pairing

All equations (3) group planes AFTER restricting to the fixed integer
fiber. Their groups and partners can depend on q. No continuation to
ambient hyperplane equality follows merely from these equations.

For a simple actual critical-cap example, let

    C=[0,1] x B_d, d>=2,

where B_d is the unit ball of volume V. Both integer centers have raw
depth V/2 and normalized depth 1/4: every cap through a center captures
at least half its own ball, while finite integer tilts isolate any desired
own half-ball. At base zero choose the two critical caps

    x_1-Lz>=0,  -x_1-Lz>=0,

and at base one choose

    x_1+L(z-1)>=0,  -x_1+L(z-1)>=0,

with L>1. Each has raw mass V/2; each opposite continuous-normal pair is
a positive circuit with kappa=1/2. At its own fiber it is an opposite pair;
at the other fiber both caps are empty. The stress pi_0=pi_1=1/2 gives
score 1/4 on both boundaries off the selected planes. Yet no two of the
four AMBIENT boundary planes are the same with opposite orientations.
This example has actual fibers, smooth strict convexity and vacuous
nontrivial compatibility. It shows directly that the conclusion must
remain fiberwise even for genuine critical caps. It is not claimed to
be a local minimum.

Even changing partners is possible for finite cap arrangements: on bases
q=0,1, use positive caps x_1>=0, x_1>=1 and negative caps
x_1<=q, x_1<=1-q, with all weights 1/4 and fibers large balls containing
both proper section planes. At base zero the first negative matches the
first positive; at base one it matches the second. The other matching
also switches. The score remains 1/2 off the planes in each fiber. These
four caps are an arrangement example, not asserted to be critical caps
of equal mass. Additional criticality constraints cannot be ignored if
one seeks a stronger cross-fiber matching theorem.

The general-body route therefore gains exact orientation-cancellation
equations on every proper cut of a fully feasible smooth strictly convex
fiber in d>=3, but no global ambient pairing or arbitrary-body extremizer
classification is inferred.
